case_studies.title: Where LLM Agents Get Stuck Debugging Databases: Access More Than Reasoning
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly asked not only to write code but to debug running systems from live runtime data. We report a field observation of one such agent (Claude Code) as it diagnosed eight database incidents in a production message-dispatch engine. In every incident whose root cause depended on runtime concurrency, the agent announced a cause, shipped a fix, and later walked it back, and each wrong guess cost a deploy-and-observe cycle. Mapping each incident to what the agent lacked, we find that access to production state was the most pervasive bottleneck. The missing access included live lock views, untruncated deadlock reports, read-only execution, and an explicit environment context. An access gap was present in all five concurrency-dependent incidents: alone in one, and in four combined with a reasoning error such as anchoring on an early cause, incomplete exploration of the configuration, or a misreading of the code's transaction semantics. The three incidents that did not depend on concurrency needed nothing beyond what the agent already had. Within the incidents, the agent's wrong hypotheses were consistent with the evidence it could see; they were not fabrications. We argue that the next step for production-debugging agents is a forensics layer that gives the agent the access it lacks inside existing security controls. Such a layer would combine a safe interrogation API, a lock-and-deadlock flight recorder, and a production replay harness.
case_studies.summary: Large‑language‑model coding agents often fail to debug database issues because they lack real‑time access to production state such as lock views and deadlock logs. The study analysed Claude Code fixing eight incidents and showed that missing production data caused repeated misdiagnoses and extra deploys. A new forensics layer could give these agents the needed state without breaking security controls.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infra that uses LLM agents for debugging, first check if your agents have a secure API to fetch live lock views and deadlock reports. Second, enable a production replay harness so the agent can run in read‑only mode with the current state. Third, monitor for repeated deploy‑and‑observe cycles – if they appear, add the forensics layer before relying on the agent for live fixes.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a real-world challenge faced by IT engineers—debugging database concurrency issues with LLM agents. It highlights practical limitations and proposes a forensic layer that could be implemented within existing security frameworks, offering a tangible service for infrastructure teams. While the agent itself is still in experimental use, the concepts are mature enough to be prototyped and deployed, and the proposed forensic layer presents clear monetisation opportunities within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Synthesis Smuggling: Maliciously Hiding Inferred Personal Attributes in LLM Outputs
case_studies.abstract: We propose Synthesis Smuggling, a novel threat model in which an adversarial LLM infers sensitive information about a user from routine assistance-seeking interactions and steganographically encodes that into innocuous-looking model-generated content. The user may then unknowingly transmit that information by sharing the generated artifact, say as an email, social-media post, or message, through ordinary communication channels. An adversary monitoring these channels can discover this information. We demonstrate this threat by training two open-weight models to infer gender and age-group labels from conversational cues and encode their predictions using invisible characters or word choices. These results show that user-shared model outputs can become a covert channel for personal inferences, even when the model itself has no direct means of contacting an adversary.
case_studies.summary: This research shows how a malicious language model can hide personal details in its outputs, turning normal messages into covert channels for attackers. It demonstrates the technique by training models to infer gender and age from conversations and embedding that info in invisible characters or word choices. The result is a stealthy way to leak user data without direct communication with the attacker.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper identifies a real security threat that could affect how IT engineers secure LLM outputs and monitor for covert channels, warranting a moderate impact score. The authors provide a working demonstration with trained models, indicating a mature system suitable for immediate testing, hence a high maturity score. While the findings could be used to build security monitoring services, the paper does not provide a clear, deployable product or API, resulting in a lower monetisation score. Overall the research is relevant, implementable, and potentially commercially useful within 90 days.

case_studies.title: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Evaluation of Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection
case_studies.abstract: Mobile GUI agents read the screen of a phone and operate apps on a user's behalf to complete multi-step tasks such as online shopping or messaging. Because the agent acts on whatever the screen shows, an attacker can embed malicious instructions into ordinary UI content and redirect its actions. We refer to this threat as environmental injection attack (EIA). Existing benchmarks measure this risk by pinning hand-crafted payloads to a fixed step of a fixed task. This approach faces two limitations. First, each payload is bound to one task in one app and does not transfer without manual redesign. Second, agents given the same task may follow different routes, so an agent that never reaches the injected page is recorded as safe without being tested. This insufficient test coverage can cause fixed-point benchmarks to underestimate the security risk of deployed mobile agents. In this work, we propose MobileProbe, a trajectory-aware red-teaming framework that evaluates mobile agents adaptively. MobileProbe discovers attacker-controllable content surfaces through automated pentesting, localizes vulnerable decision points along the agent's trajectory, and iteratively refines context-aware payloads through a surrogate-filtered evolutionary loop. We construct a benchmark of 83 long-horizon attack instances spanning 12 mobile applications. Each is annotated with a Confidentiality, Integrity, or Availability (CIA) attack goal to cover the principal categories of security threats facing mobile agents. On three representative agent architectures, MobileProbe attains higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM, and prior automated red-teaming baselines adapted to the mobile domain. MobileProbe can serve as a pre-deployment auditing tool to systematically uncover vulnerabilities and inform security hardening of mobile agents.
case_studies.summary: MobileProbe is an automated testing tool that finds hidden security risks in mobile app‑automation agents by injecting malicious content during their task execution. It builds a trajectory‑aware framework that automatically discovers vulnerable points, crafts adaptive payloads, and tests 83 real‑world scenarios across 12 apps, beating existing methods in finding attacks. This work is relevant for anyone deploying or managing mobile automation – it offers a practical auditing tool to spot and fix security holes before launch.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage mobile automation agents, use MobileProbe to run automated penetration tests: 1. Integrate MobileProbe into your CI pipeline to scan new agent builds. 2. Review the identified attack paths and harden those UI surfaces. 3. Re‑run tests after changes to confirm vulnerabilities are mitigated.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a concrete security risk for mobile agents that could impact IT engineers managing mobile device security. The framework is described as a prototype with a benchmark, but no public code or deployed system is reported, so maturity is moderate. The approach could be turned into a security testing service within 90 days, giving it good monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications
case_studies.abstract: Affected-version ranges in vulnerability databases decide which deployments scanners, patching pipelines, and incident responders treat as vulnerable, yet these ranges are often incomplete, so vulnerable releases are silently treated as safe. Auditing them requires executable evidence: given a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a listed version, show that the same vulnerability can be triggered on an earlier, unlisted version. This cross-version PoC migration combines source-code analysis, environment repair, and execution-based verification. We introduce CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 migration instances across 45 CVEs in the Python web ecosystem. Each instance includes a version-pinned container, a reference PoC, and a vulnerability-specific oracle; two validators check that the observed effect arises from the disclosed vulnerability. Benchmark construction confirms 149 vulnerable prior versions absent from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations (nine models and two harnesses), the best configuration resolves 58.3% of instances, compared with 8.7% for an adapted trace-guided baseline. Attack-vector shifts are particularly difficult: no configuration resolves more than 37.9% of these instances. Higher resolve rates are associated with a smaller share of missed-API failures and a larger share of incomplete executions among the remaining failures. In one configuration, withholding the reference PoC and its environment specification reduces resolve rate from 50.4% to 15.0%, highlighting the value of the supplied reference package. CrossPloit provides an execution-based measurement of under-reported exposure and of how far its enumeration can be automated.
case_studies.summary: Many vulnerability databases miss older releases of Python web applications, leaving them mistakenly marked as safe. CrossPloit builds a benchmark of 127 real-world cases, proving that 149 earlier versions were in fact vulnerable and that a specialised migration approach can validate over half of these cases. This shows that your vulnerability scanning and patching pipelines may need to be checked for hidden exposure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage Python web apps, first cross‑check your affected‑version lists against the CrossPloit findings; then run a cross‑version PoC migration on any version flagged as missing to confirm exposure; finally, integrate the benchmark’s validation step into your CI pipeline to catch silent vulnerabilities.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses cross-version PoC migration for Python web apps, directly impacting vulnerability assessment workflows used by IT engineers. It provides a benchmark and some trained models, but lacks a fully deployed system, hence moderate maturity. The reference PoC packages could be packaged into a service for rapid vulnerability validation, yielding some monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
case_studies.abstract: Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.
case_studies.summary: GPU workloads for LLMs suffer from power overshoot spikes that cause throttling and inconsistent performance. The authors built hardware and firmware controls that smooth these power peaks, boosting performance by 3‑12 % over existing GPU power‑management solutions. This can directly improve the reliability and speed of your GPU‑based ML services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage GPU‑based ML workloads, 1) audit your GPU power‑management logs for transient power spikes; 2) upgrade to firmware that includes fine‑grained power‑management to dampen spikes; 3) monitor performance gains to ensure 3‑12 % improvement is realised.
case_studies.relevance_tag: GPU power management for AI workloads
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper tackles GPU power management for LLM workloads, which is relevant to infrastructure engineers managing GPU clusters. However, the work appears to be experimental, with no released code or production deployment, and the monetisation potential is limited due to lack of ready-to-use tooling.
